claims.claim_text: For a hardware design published openly, a registered trademark on the product name is the only protection that remains available: it stops a competitor using the name, but it does not stop them copying the printed circuit board or the rest of the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only way I can protect it is to, um, or, or you, if you're making your open hardware product is to trademark the name and then they're not allowed to use the name, but they can copy your PCB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: A patent and an open-source hardware release disclose different things. The patent publishes the invention as described and claimed, but not the files needed to build the product; an open-source hardware release gives away the schematic, the PCB files and the bill of materials in full.
claims.quote_verbatim: the patent, you don't actually give away all of your actual, uh, files to manufacture it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: Invention-promotion firms that advertise to market an inventor's idea make their money by signing the inventor up for expensive patent filings and taking a large share of any proceeds, rather than by selling the invention.
claims.quote_verbatim: All they do is, um, make you sign up for ridiculous, expensive patents. And they, they take a huge cut out of it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Pursuing a patent as an individual inventor can consume hundreds of thousands of dollars without producing a return: an Australian inventor of a mains outlet with a built-in USB socket is described as having spent that much on obtaining a patent, and the idea was subsequently built by everyone anyway.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think he spent like hundreds of thousands of dollars trying to patent the damn thing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rigorous engineering stuff may be out the window

claims.claim_text: Marking a product with patent numbers that have expired can expose the manufacturer to a penalty assessed per unit sold, reportedly on the order of a hundred dollars an item, which is why patent markings are removed once the underlying patents lapse; Fluke's revised 87 multimeter dropped the patent numbers that appeared on the back of earlier units.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually get fined for putting expired patent numbers on a product. You can get fined like a hundred bucks per item
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: A patent's term runs about twenty years, after which the disclosed design is free to build. The original Xilinx FPGA patents, naming Ross Freeman as inventor, had passed that point, so the early parts they covered could be reproduced by anyone.
claims.quote_verbatim: What's expired is a patent that's more than 20 years old.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Filing a patent application does not mean a patent will issue. One hardware engineer who went through the process had every application refused, and described prosecution as long, drawn out and tedious.
claims.quote_verbatim: None of mine were issued. It's a, it's a long drawn out, annoying process.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Patent portfolios are themselves a principal asset in large acquisitions: Google's purchase of Motorola was stated by Larry Page to be substantially about acquiring its patents, a holding of roughly sixteen thousand.
claims.quote_verbatim: he outright said a big part of it is we want their patents. I think it was 16,000 patents they had
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: One route out of federally funded university research into a company is to file first and license second: the founders of Cree wrote ten patents covering the silicon carbide technology they had invented, then asked North Carolina State University for an exclusive licence in exchange for stock in the new company, which the university cleared with the funding agency.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first thing we did is we wrote 10 patents on the technology
claims.speaker: John Edmond
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: Patents were only part of what kept silicon carbide LED manufacturing to a single company; the larger part was vertical integration, having started the company around both silicon carbide LEDs and silicon carbide electronics so that no one else could produce the material.
claims.quote_verbatim: Well, that's part of it. But the other part of it is we vertically integrated.
claims.speaker: John Edmond
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: Patent literature works as a process-engineering reference. An experimenter reproduced coffee decaffeination by reading the relevant patents through Google Patents, where the process is set out in detail, although patent prose is generally hard to read.
claims.quote_verbatim: the entire coffee decaffeination process is spelled out in super high detail in all the patents
claims.speaker: Ben Krasnow
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow - Sprauncy Saccadic Spintherism

claims.claim_text: Older Texas Instruments patents disclose far more than the claimed invention, including complete schematics for a calculator chip and the code it ran, which makes the back catalogue a usable trove for reverse-engineering old silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll have like pages and pages of entire schematics for the calculator chip, all the source code that the chip is running
claims.speaker: Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: An engineer with roughly two dozen patents assigned to AMD and Xilinx received a commemorative plaque for each one; recognition rather than payment is the usual reward attached to inventions assigned to a large employer.
claims.quote_verbatim: I got a plaque for each one.
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Patent fights between two comparably resourced competitors tend not to end in exclusion. Xilinx and Altera litigated against each other repeatedly and settled by cross-licensing their portfolios once the legal spend outweighed the benefit.
claims.quote_verbatim: get resolved eventually by cross-licensing all the patents
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: A semiconductor company should expect to be sued for infringement eventually regardless of whether it set out to infringe anything, which is the stated reason for holding patents at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're a semiconductor company, at some point, guess what? You're going to get sued.
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: A patent portfolio functions simultaneously as defence and offence: holdings are trading stock in a dispute, and once a portfolio is large enough the holder can initiate assertions rather than only answer them.
claims.quote_verbatim: the more portfolio patents you have, the more you have to trade
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Laboratory notebook discipline at defence contractors required every page to be written in pen, dated and signed, with unused space on a part-filled page struck through so that nothing could be inserted later and back-dated.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you didn't fill the page, you were to scribble out all of the blank space on the page so that you couldn't go back and post edit later
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Under the first-to-invent system the inventor carried the burden of proving the date of conception, which is why contemporaneous witnessed and dated notebook entries mattered.
claims.quote_verbatim: the burden of proof was on you
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The United States moved from first-to-invent to first-to-file, so priority turns on the date an application reaches the patent office rather than on proof of when the invention was conceived; the evidentiary demand on dated notebooks fell accordingly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it just switched over first to file versus first to invent
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Holding a granted patent is not by itself decisive in a dispute; the outcome turns heavily on how much each side can afford to spend on counsel.
claims.quote_verbatim: The person with the most money and the best lawyers generally always wins.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Deliberately not searching for patents does not protect a designer: not knowing that a patent covers, for example, a standard backplane or test connector arrangement is not a defence to infringement.
claims.quote_verbatim: ignorance is not a defense in the patent world
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A patent holder asserting a stereolithography patent sued not only the company building the printer but also the crowdfunding platform selling it, on the theory that the sales channel was aiding the infringement; a distribution channel can be named alongside the manufacturer.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're not only suing Formlabs, but they're suing Kickstarter
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Publishing a design is put forward as an alternative to filing on it: once the work is public it stands as prior art, making it harder for anyone else to obtain a patent over the same ground.
claims.quote_verbatim: why bother patenting when you can just publish it first
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: Defensive-publication repositories exist specifically so that an idea can be placed on the public record as prior art, which is more reliable than relying on a personal blog post to establish the date and the disclosure.
claims.quote_verbatim: a website that was set up specifically as a repository to publish your ideas as prior art
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: Defensive publication secures no rights for the publisher. It cannot be converted into a patent later; its only function is to keep the ground clear so that others cannot obtain one.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not that you're going to be able to patent it either. It's just trying to hold other people off
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: Prior art on the public record does not prevent a suit from being filed. The defence still has to be argued, and pointing at a prior-art publication does not by itself end the matter.
claims.quote_verbatim: Their lawyers aren't going to care. They're still going to try and sue your ass.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCBs, Tektronix & Ham Radio - Habitual Handicraft Hangups

claims.claim_text: Large-company patenting is driven by aggregate portfolio weight rather than by the value of any individual invention; the relevant comparison is how many patents each side holds.
claims.quote_verbatim: the patent business for them is not so much about the IP and the patents as it's just the overall throw weight of who has, you know, how many patents
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Davidson - Hoodied HP Hijinks

claims.claim_text: Venture investors assess a hardware startup partly on what barrier surrounds its technology, and a patent portfolio contributes to that assessment alongside content kept as trade secret inside an ASIC or FPGA.
claims.quote_verbatim: what kind of moat do we have around our tech? And a patent portfolio is part of that
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: A funded startup may file principally to satisfy investors rather than to protect anything: the count of patents held is among the first questions asked in a venture round, so applications are filed to make the company attractive.
claims.quote_verbatim: I wouldn't do them if I didn't have to. But we have to make the company look attractive.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: For a one-person business the economics of patenting do not close: filing is expensive, and an infringement cannot be pursued without the funds to litigate. One such engineer abandoned patenting in favour of publishing designs openly and staying ahead by continuing to release new products.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's expensive to do it. And then, you know, even if I, somebody did infringe on my patent, I'm like, I had no money to sue them
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: The cost of enforcement puts patents out of practical reach well above hobbyist scale: an engineer running a ten-million-dollar company judged that he still could not afford to sue a copier.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if I was a $10 million company and I had a patent on something and somebody copied it, I wouldn't be able to afford to sue them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The case in which a patent is judged to pay off for a small engineering business is a startup being acquired by a larger company, rather than protection of a product in the market.
claims.quote_verbatim: they help if we're entrepreneurial and we're doing a startup and we want to get bought by a biggie
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The commonly quoted figures are about ten thousand dollars to obtain a patent and about a hundred thousand to defend it the first time, with the patent only demonstrating its value once it has survived that defence.
claims.quote_verbatim: what they say is $10,000 to get a patent. But $100,000 to defend it for the first time and then it's worth something
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: A startup should not place its emphasis on intellectual property or assume that a strong patent position will keep competitors out; on the account of a founder who ran several failed startups, value is the idea multiplied by the execution, and a good idea executed poorly is worth little.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to protect your intellectual property, but I wouldn't put my emphasis there or think that I was going to, you know, keep everybody out because of my great IP
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Where the underlying technique is long known, a patent is obtained by scoping the claims to a specific application. A patent pending on transferring data to a device by flashing light was directed at configuring Wi-Fi credentials, because sending data with modulated light was not new.
claims.quote_verbatim: the patent is really geared more towards using it for wifi setup
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: The bargain in a patent is publication in exchange for the right to exclude: the document is public and anyone may read it, but using what it describes exposes the user to suit. A company that announces it is releasing its patents is therefore committing not to sue, not disclosing anything that was not already published.
claims.quote_verbatim: by definition, a patent is open source. Well, it's open, right? It's open. You can go read it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tesla, Checklists and Bullies - Emerging External Eupsychics

claims.claim_text: There is a gap between what a rights holder's lawyers assert and what is enforceable. Anyone with funds and motive can bring a suit however weak, and the defendant can be ruined by the cost of defending it before a court reaches the merits.
claims.quote_verbatim: Anyone at any time can sue you for absolutely anything, regardless if it's valid.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tesla, Checklists and Bullies - Emerging External Eupsychics

claims.claim_text: Because a granted patent's disclosure is public, describing or republishing what it teaches is not the infringing act; what the patent restricts is making and selling the claimed invention in competition with the holder.
claims.quote_verbatim: The definition of a patent is that the information is publicly available. You can rehash and republish that as long as you don't make money from it and compete.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Robots are coming - Ominous Operational Overhaul

claims.claim_text: A patentable invention need not exist as hardware. An application can be granted on a conceptual design that was never constructed, and the requirement to furnish a working model belongs to an earlier era of patent practice.
claims.quote_verbatim: patents don't need to be built
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Voja Antonic - Gerontogenous Galaksija Genesis

claims.claim_text: Off-the-shelf conductive inks formulated for inkjet deposition are heavily patented, which restricts how far a company using them can develop its own formulation, and they are priced at the cost of bulk silver plus processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: because they're already commercially available, they're heavily patented, which means you can't really move much on your own
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: United States patent suits concentrated in one federal district in Texas because its local procedural rules favoured plaintiffs, which is where entities asserting patents established a presence.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's actually a single court in Texas, like some district in Texas, where, like, every patent suit is filed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: A United States Supreme Court ruling reaffirmed a 1957 decision holding that the Patent Act requires a patent suit to be brought where the defendant company is incorporated, overriding the broader general venue rules and requiring a genuine corporate presence in a district before a suit can be raised there.
claims.quote_verbatim: the specific rules of the Patent Act, which require a plaintiff to sue companies where they are incorporated
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Filing rather than keeping a technique secret is a real tradeoff in silicon design: a patent publishes how the result was achieved, which lets competitors design around it, so one school of thought inside semiconductor companies holds that a circuit trick is better hidden in the die and simply shipped.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you patent something, it becomes public and people can see how you did it
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: Large semiconductor companies apply internal pressure to generate patentable work, but screen disclosures before filing: committees review proposed applications to check they make sense rather than filing everything submitted.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have committees of people that look through the patents to make sure that they make sense before we even apply for it
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: A common filing strategy is to take a single underlying idea and file on many variant implementations of it, so that the coverage extends beyond the one embodiment actually built.
claims.quote_verbatim: You come up with one idea and then you patent 10 ways to do it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An engineering research group oriented towards technology transfer files patent applications before chasing publications, inverting the order followed by groups whose objective is a high-profile journal paper.
claims.quote_verbatim: we look to patent things first, frankly. We like to do tech transfer. So, we first look to patent. And then we do all the publication hunting.
claims.speaker: Jonathan Ellis

claims.claim_text: A semiconductor patent has value only if somebody will take a licence to it, which frequently means going after a company and entering litigation to get there; applications are sometimes filed with no development done and no demonstration that the concept works.
claims.quote_verbatim: with a patent, especially in semiconductors, it's only worth something if someone will license it from you
claims.speaker: Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: In a downturn or on the way out of business, a company may hand its patent portfolio to a venture capital firm; for the firm to recover its money it then asserts those patents against companies that are making products, sometimes on legitimate grounds and sometimes not.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll go to a venture capital company with their patent portfolio and say, save us
claims.speaker: Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: Patent rights are national. A granted patent gives the holder the right to block importation into the country that granted it and to sue there, and confers nothing in countries where no corresponding patent was obtained.
claims.quote_verbatim: it basically gives you the right to block importing into whatever country where you have the patent once you once the patent is granted
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Open-source hardware makes some venture investors uneasy, and the question that follows is what patent protection and what portfolio the company has.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of VCs get scared when you're open source
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Not every investor treats a patent position as a selling point: one investor pushes back on founders who lead with their patents, on the ground that the money is meant to fund building a product rather than litigation.
claims.quote_verbatim: I basically look at them and I say, I'm not here to fund a lawsuit
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: A patent filed on the self-balancing hoverboard was weak against prior art because the Shenzhen supply ecosystem was already mass-producing every part needed, including self-balancing unicycles and electric scooters; the combination, not any new development, was the only novelty claimed.
claims.quote_verbatim: that ecosystem had every single part already in mass production needed to build a self-balancing hoverboard
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang

claims.claim_text: On the account of a designer who sold an open-source laptop, a product can be monetised for long enough to fund the next generation without strong patent or copyright protection, at the cost of having to stay competitive rather than sitting on a granted monopoly.
claims.quote_verbatim: even without sort of really strong patent or copyright protection, I'm able to sort of monetize my ideas for a period of time
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang

claims.claim_text: Patents brought into a company are assigned to it as a condition of taking investment. An inventor who received patents from a former employer and then raised capital no longer owned them, holding shares in the company that did.
claims.quote_verbatim: she has signed over the rights to when she took all the investment capital in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Before cloning a mechanical part, both utility patents and design patents on it need checking, since they are separate instruments with separate terms. An engineer who verified that the design patents on the Lego Technic beams he was reproducing had expired noted that expiry has not stopped the rights holder from suing.
claims.quote_verbatim: The design patents, um, have expired for the parts that I'm, uh, checking out. However, that hasn't stopped Lego from suing people
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: A patent attorney's opening move with a prospective client is to ask what the patent is for. Patents are expensive business instruments used to protect an asset so that it can be sold, and carry little practical meaning for an individual who simply wants one.
claims.quote_verbatim: I always start, start down the road of no, no, you don't want a patent. What are you going to do with the patent?
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: There is no lightweight, automatically arising form of patent protection, but publishing or open-sourcing a design achieves part of the same end: the publication is prior art, so others cannot obtain a patent on the same thing.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you publish something, you're kind of short circuiting other people's patenting
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: Copyright arises automatically at the moment a work is created and trademark exists in an unregistered common-law form marked with TM, whereas patents have no equivalent instantaneous or unregistered form and must be applied for.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you push the button on your camera and take a picture, you own the copyright on that picture. You own it the very second you created it
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: The process begins with a disclosure meeting at which the inventor explains the invention to the attorney, and the inventor should be able to state what has been invented in a single sentence before the drafting starts.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want to be able to tell the patent attorney I've invented this and spit it out in one sentence
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: The attorney's core task is translation of scope: the inventor describes the invention in engineering terms and the attorney drafts claims that capture it as broadly as the art allows, deliberately avoiding the specific vocabulary an engineer would use, so that the resulting rights cover more than the one embodiment.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'll describe your invention to me in engineering terms, and then I will write claims that try to capture it as broadly as possible
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: Specific numeric limits written into a claim are what let a competitor design around it. A claim reciting a level of 3.3 to 3.5 volts is escaped by building the same product at 3.6 volts, which is why claim drafting avoids concrete quantities such as voltage levels wherever possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: your claim says, you know, okay, so it has three voltage levels and one of them is 3.3 to 3.5 volts. Well, I could just design mine to always use 3.6 volts. Now your patent does not apply to my product.
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: When the examiner cites art that reads on a broad claim, prosecution proceeds by amending to the least restrictive limitation that still clears the art. Faced with a reference showing twelve and nine volt levels, the claim is narrowed to something like less than twelve volts rather than to the applicant's actual values.
claims.quote_verbatim: we would say, okay, well, less than 12 volts, right. To get around the prior art
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: In a field that has been worked for decades, such as computation or communications, the broad claims were taken long ago and what remains is infill: no longer a car or a car with two axles, but the tread pattern on a tyre and how its depth varies from middle to side.
claims.quote_verbatim: once an area of technology has been around for a while, like let's say computation or communication systems, you're doing a lot of infill
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: Press and trade-journal articles reporting that a company has patented something are usually wrong in some subtlety, and a case is then built on the misreading; patent documents are confusing to non-specialists and headlines about them should not be taken at face value.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you look at patents as a, you know, as a non-patent expert, they're confusing
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: An engineer working in a narrow technical field should be reading the patents in that field, since the disclosure obligation is what the public gets in return for the grant; the caveat is that some are written strangely, some do not mean what they appear to say, and some are simply wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: if there's a very specific area of technology you're interested in, you should be reading the patents in that area
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: Applications drafted by the inventor without an attorney, known as pro se filings, are characterised by poor claims even when the underlying invention is sound, since claim scope is the part of the document that requires the specialist skill.
claims.quote_verbatim: patents that are what we call pro se patents where the, where they're written by the inventor themselves because the claim, the claims are just usually so bad
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: The proportion of ideas that justify a patent rounds to zero. What carries value is not the idea but its business implementation, and protection is worth pursuing only once that implementation exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ideas aren't valuable. It's their implementation, their business implementation that's valuable
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: A ten-thousand-dollar retainer quoted up front is used by patent firms as a filter on individual inventors, and it is small against what prosecuting an application actually costs; inventors who accept it usually have a concrete business reason for filing.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the thing is, if you end up doing something for them, that $10,000 is going to be nothing.
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: Experienced patent attorneys prefer corporate clients such as large technology companies that file in volume, write cheques and need no hand-holding, and avoid independent inventors, who demand attention and are the source of malpractice claims.
claims.quote_verbatim: they never want to deal with independent inventors
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: Among small companies, the practical purpose of filing is value signalling to investors: a portfolio demonstrates that the company has invented specific things, and is filed to support fundraising or an acquisition rather than to be enforced.
claims.quote_verbatim: of the smaller companies, like the startups I work with, it's all about getting funding
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: For a company raising twenty to eighty million dollars against a steep burn rate, spending on the order of a hundred thousand dollars on a patent portfolio is proportionate, because the outcome is binary: if the company succeeds it needs the patents, and if it fails it had nothing to lose anyway.
claims.quote_verbatim: to, to put a hundred thousand dollars or whatever into developing a patent portfolio is probably pretty wise and your investors are going to love it
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: A patent confers negative rights only. It gives the holder no right to make or sell anything; it gives the ability to stop someone else, which is worth having only if the holder is willing and able to sue.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're a bundle of negative rights. So they don't give you a right to do anything. They give you the ability to stop someone else from doing it.
claims.speaker: Joe Long

claims.claim_text: The first question a prospective licensee asks an inventor is whether there is a patent, so an inventor intending to license rather than manufacture generally needs one before the negotiation starts.
claims.quote_verbatim: The first thing they're going to ask you, if you try to license something, they're going to say, do you have a patent?
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: A licensee's reasoning for demanding a patent is its own development spend: it will not commit something like half a million dollars to bringing an easily copied product to market with no protection against immediate knock-offs.
claims.quote_verbatim: why should we, why should we invest a half million dollars in developing this when it's going to be knocked off right away?
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: A patent strengthens the inventor's negotiating position in a licensing deal and, once the product is on the market, can deter competitors and knock-off manufacturers from entering.
claims.quote_verbatim: It gives you a much stronger, uh, negotiating position when you're trying to license something
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: The protection a patent delivers in practice is limited, because there are frequently ways to design around the claims.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are very often ways to get around patents, so they don't always give you all that much protection
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Obviousness is the routine ground on which applications are refused during prosecution, and it is difficult to argue against because anything looks obvious once it has been seen. An inventor with twenty-two or twenty-three granted patents described this as the recurring friction of the process.
claims.quote_verbatim: they keep rejecting me saying that my idea is obvious
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: MEMS ultrasound transducers are held under patents by a small number of companies and laboratories developing them, and cannot be bought in ones and twos by an engineer wanting to build a kit around them.
claims.quote_verbatim: Cause they're all super patented into these.
claims.speaker: Jean Rintoul

claims.claim_text: In the Australian system as described by one practitioner, an initial filing made when an idea looks promising opens a twelve-month window in which the full application must follow, so the first filing buys a period of protected secrecy rather than granting rights outright.
claims.quote_verbatim: you drop a patent in when you, when you think you've got a good idea in the Australian system. That means we've got 12 months to then put a full provisional in
claims.speaker: Paul Thompson

claims.claim_text: An idea as such is not patentable; what is claimed is a particular method of implementing it, which is why narrow implementation differences can each carry their own patent.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't patent the idea, but you can patent your method of doing it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rigorous engineering stuff may be out the window

claims.claim_text: A gallium nitride device maker facing a state-funded Chinese competitor set up to imitate its products asserted its patents against that competitor, and the dispute ran simultaneously in several countries.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've definitely taken them to task with our patents. And we're locked in patent battles in a couple of different countries
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: On the account of a device maker enforcing patents internationally, the United States is the hardest jurisdiction in which to enforce a patent, and China, Germany and Japan are all easier; that ordering is described as having reversed over the previous fifteen to twenty years.
claims.quote_verbatim: The hardest place to enforce your patent is the United States of America.
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: The cost of United States enforcement comes from repeated challenge in parallel forums: a win at the International Trade Commission can be followed by proceedings at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, in the customs office and in federal court, each with its own appeals, with no bar on bringing the same challenge again.
claims.quote_verbatim: people can challenge patents in multiple forums, multiple times
claims.speaker: Alex Lidow
claims.episode_title: Inventing the Power MOSFET with Alex Lidow

claims.claim_text: A startup with a successful product should expect competitors to weigh buying it against copying it, and a patent alone is only a document without the legal team to enforce it; the durable barrier described in that instance was building the sensor in a silicon process at fine pitch and volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: sure you have patents, but that's a piece of paper, man
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: The Terahertz Frontier with Greg Charvat of Teradar

claims.claim_text: Assertion of a patent works largely as a threat: the holder sends a lawyer's letter and hopes the recipient backs down, because a recipient with money to fight can simply refuse and the holder may not be able to afford the case.
claims.quote_verbatim: If somebody does your thing, you go, I've got a patent on this, right? So you send them a threatening letter from your lawyer.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Can't We All Just Get Arduino? - Tardiloquent Trademark Tirade
